comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
I'm 99% sure it's a network or system misconfiguration. Maybe a firewall issue... I've heard of lots of issues like this on our forum, and almost always the solution is to eliminate all other external factors (CDN, firewalls, port forwarding, etc) and re-introduce them one by one and see where it breaks.

We're glad that you're using Caddy! So far, this doesn't look like a bug in Caddy. It looks more like a question about how to use Caddy rather than a bug.

Since this issue tracker is reserved for actionable development items, I'm going to close this, but we have a [community forum at caddy.community](https://caddy.community) where more people will be exposed to your question, including people who may be more expert or experienced than I am with the specific issue you're facing. I hope you'll ask your question there. The Help category in the forum even provides a template you can fill out.

If I'm wrong, and this does turn out to be a bug after further investigation, we can reopen this. :+1: If you do figure it out yourself, let us know what solved it!

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
Alright, cURL with the verbose flag is very helpful right now. What I've learned so far is that:

- Connecting over HTTP redirects to HTTPS with a status code 308, as it should.
- cURL can complete the TLS handshake and maintain a connection to the server.

Interestingly, however, it seems to freeze at `* TLSv1.3 (OUT), TLS handshake, Client hello (1):`, and never gets the response from Caddy, which supports what the Caddy logs were showing. It seems to get through the entire TLS handshake fine, and then never send the response. I'm going to keep looking into this but I have almost no idea where to go from here.

Edit: quick question, would there be any way to see if Caddy is actually sending data? I'm beginning to suspect there may be something blocking the response data.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
Alright, I've narrowed down the issue even farther. If I send a normal HTTP request, everything works flawlessly. The moment TLS is brought into the equation, however, it completely breaks. There's something wrong with the TLS connection specifically, but I'm not sure what it is.

For whatever reason, when TLS is enabled, the server just times out.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
So, I hate to tell you, I can't reproduce the problem. That site loads instantly just fine for me here. (over TLS)

The good news is, it likely isn't a Caddy bug. Something about the network in between you and the server...

> Edit: quick question, would there be any way to see if Caddy is actually sending data? 

The logs will say how much was written in an HTTP response. But there's no way to know how much of it got delivered really. TCP is supposed to do this but network stacks in the middle can make pretty much anything on the wire misleading.

The best way to know if data is actually flowing at the low/raw packet level is a packet capture with Wireshark or similar. Ideally on both client and server.

I know I said I wouldn't post any more updates, but I've decided to just give up on this. I'll set up a new subdomain, and it'll work for a few seconds before breaking (with the exception of `test.tbuk.me`, for whatever reason), but when setting up a basic caddy + code-server install on one of my other Linux machines on a different network, it worked flawlessly. The only things that I think could be happening are:

1. Both networks use different ISPs, so it could be the ISP blocking the TLS (for some reason)
2. The Debian install on the other machine is broken, and I'll need to reinstall it.
3. There's something broken in Caddy on specifically that server, that persists after reinstalls.

Both are really annoying to deal with, but given that the first option is impossible for me to ever resolve, and the 3rd option is ridiculously unlikely, I think I'll just go with the 2nd option and back up the server's data before nuking it and starting fresh. If that doesn't fix it, there's no hope of me running an in-home server at this house again, so it wouldn't matter anyway.

It would help to know though, are there any files left-over from Caddy when you `apt purge` it and reinstall it? My previous domain was `tbuk.site`, but I wanted a cheaper domain so I switched it, and I'm wondering if the name similarity could be causing issues?

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
# I FIGURED IT OUT
So, yeah, I figured it out, and I'm pretty sure it is a bug with how TLS certificates are handled.

When I was thinking about potential issues (I really didn't want to reset the whole server). I was incredibly confused as to why `test.tbuk.site` was working, as that was disproving the fact that there's an issue with the Linux install, and then I thought about what I wrote in the last part of my last comment, and that's when I realized, **I had never used that subdomain before.** `test.tbuk.tld` was never a subdomain I had used under the `tbuk.site` domain. After realizing this, I tested my theory by putting in a random string of characters so I was sure it was definitely never used by me, and sure enough, it worked flawlessly. I never noticed this, though, because I was just switching domains. I wanted to keep everything at the same subdomain, and didn't add any new services, so I never saw that.

When I switch back to a subdomain I also had under `tbuk.site`, it fails again. There seems to be some sort of conflict due to the similarity of the domains(?) that is causing some sort of TLS handshake issue and preventing a connection. So, while the issue is mostly resolved, I still want to be able to use a subdomain I used at some point in the long period of time I owned that previous domain, and that's where the issue comes in. This also applies to `nginx`. This isn't an issue exclusive to Caddy, it's an issue with TLS on my server in general, which confuses me even more. Is there a bug involving OpenSSL? Why do duplicate subdomains on _similar_ domains cause an issue?

tl;dr, for anyone with the same obscure issue I'm having, something within Linux doesn't like handling SSL certificates for duplicate subdomains that share the same domain, only with a different TLD. If all you change is the TLD, SSL/TLS handshakes will never complete, for whatever reason. In other words, if you have the URL `test.example.com`, you can't remove that from Caddy/nginx and switch to using `test.example.net`, you have to have a unique subdomain despite them having different TLDs, and not being hosted at the same time.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
Adding to this again, the trick I did last time of using unique subdomains didn't do anything this time around. Sometimes it times out at `* TLSv1.3 (IN), TLS handshake, Newsession Ticket (4)`, other times at `* TLSv1.3 (OUT), TLS handshake, Client hello (1)`, and sometimes it makes it completely through, only to start timing out on the next request.

This is a really infuriating issue because it's practically impossible to debug. The server is on a fiber gigabit network, so there's no chance of any network issues (especially considering I can still access it through ngrok), the server isn't under any load, and things that aren't HTTP such as SSH, SFTP, and VNC work perfectly fine. I've gone as far as disabling my router's firewall, the servers firewall, and all of Cloudflare's security (only temporarily, don't worry) to see if there was anything blocking it in the middle, but there isn't, it still fails. It's something to do with the software on that specific server, and I can't figure it out. The last thing left to try is go the nuclear route and completely reinstall Linux on the server and start from scratch (which I'm not sure how I could do remotely).

The good news is, this issue seems to be very easy to reproduce, given the fact that this is the second time it's happened under the same conditions.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
Hey devs, I think this may actually be a Caddy issue. After enabling debug mode and reading the full logs, checking cURL in --trace-ascii mode and -v mode, and using tcpdump to check traffic on port 443, it all seems to indicate that the TLS handshake completes perfectly. The issue is when it gets to the HTTP/2 request.

Once the HTTP/2 request is made, no matter what device/IP it comes from, or what software it comes from, Caddy very rarely responds. Occasionally it will respond once, but then fail to respond to any requests again for hours, which makes me highly doubt it's a network configuration issue (I mean, what kind of network issue only occurs with one server on the network, and randomly decides whether to allow HTTP requests and filter nothing else).

I really have no idea what the problem could be, but it's incredibly clear it's a webserver problem given that SSH, SFTP, VNC, and game servers all still work perfectly.

test.example.net {
